evals.prompt: My haunted-carnival game needs music. Write me a title theme and a battle loop that share a motif: the title should feel like a sad, out-of-tune calliope waltz with nobody on the rides, and the battle track fast and driving, like a NES boss fight with a bit of 16-bit polish. Both must loop seamlessly. Also a short 'you died' stinger. Put the WAVs in ./audio and keep whatever script you write so I can tweak the tunes later.
evals.expected_output: Three audio files in ./audio (title loop, battle loop, death stinger) produced by a seeded generator script that stays in the repo; the two loops wrap without a seam; the stinger starts and ends in silence; the two loops share a recognisable motif (same note sequence, transposed or re-timed); the generator separates the composition from the instruments and writes MIDI of the composition.
expectations: Three WAV (or OGG) files exist under ./audio: a title loop, a battle loop and a death stinger
Both loops pass a seam check: the jump from the last sample back to the first is no bigger than 1.5 times the clip's 99th-percentile sample step, and neither clips (peak under -0.1 dBFS)
The stinger starts at silence and ends in silence (last 5 ms under 1% of peak)
A Python generator script was written and kept in the repo, seeds its randomness, and regenerates identical files when run again
The title is in 3/4 (a waltz grid: 3 beats per bar) at a slow tempo and the battle track is at 130 bpm or faster
The title and the battle cue share a motif: the same sequence of at least four pitch intervals appears in both scores (allowing transposition and different note lengths)
The generator keeps the composition (patterns/notes) separate from the instrument choice (voices/effects), so instruments can be swapped without editing the note patterns
A .mid file of each cue's composition was written
The music RMS is between -20 and -12 dBFS for both loops and the stinger peaks between -6 and -1 dBFS
The final message tells the user it could not listen, gives the levels, and names concrete things to listen for or tweak

evals.prompt: I'm prototyping a 16-bit style sci-fi adventure (think SNES era). Graybox the soundtrack for me: an exploration loop, a tension loop for when the alarm is on, and a victory jingle. Placeholder instruments are fine for now, I just want to hear the tunes. Then, as a separate second step, give me a 'dressed' version with proper 16-bit-style instruments and effects without changing the tunes at all; I need to be able to prove the composition didn't change between the two versions. Output into ./soundtrack/graybox and ./soundtrack/dressed.
evals.expected_output: Two renders of each of the three cues (graybox and dressed) in the two folders; MIDI files of the compositions that are byte-identical between the two passes; a generator whose scores are untouched by the dressing pass (only kits/instrument mappings changed); the dressed versions use different voices and effects (echo, pad, FM or similar) from the graybox; loops seamless and the jingle a clean one-shot.
expectations: Both ./soundtrack/graybox and ./soundtrack/dressed contain an exploration loop, a tension loop and a victory jingle
For each cue, a MIDI file exists for both passes and the two files are byte-identical (or a single MIDI is shared with the agent showing a hash proving it did not change)
The note patterns / score definitions in the generator are identical between the two passes (a diff of the scores is empty; only instrument/kit definitions differ)

The dressed render of each cue differs audibly from the graybox: different voices or effects (for example echo, a pad, FM bass, reverb), verified by the generator's kit definitions and by the files not being identical
All four loops (two per pass) pass the seam check and the two jingles start and end in silence
The tension loop is distinguishable from the exploration loop in character: faster tempo, denser rhythm or darker harmony per the score definitions
The agent explains the graybox/dressed contract to the user: scores fixed, kits swapped, MIDI as the proof
The generator script runs from the command line and regenerates both passes (e.g. a --graybox flag or two kit sets)

evals.prompt: Make the sound effects for my card-duel game: card played, card drawn, shuffle, lose a heart, win the duel, lose the duel, and a soft two-note blip when a character starts talking. Retro feel (bleepy, like an old console), consistent loudness across the set, mono WAVs into ./sfx. They have to come out identical if I run the script again.
evals.expected_output: Seven mono WAV one-shots in ./sfx made by one seeded Python script; each starts and ends in silence without clipping; levels are consistent (peaks within a few dB, quieter things like the talk blip deliberately quieter); the voices are synthesised (pulse/square tones, noise bursts, modal hits), not sampled; re-running the script reproduces the same bytes.
expectations: Seven WAV files exist in ./sfx: card played, card drawn, shuffle, lose a heart, win, lose, talk blip
Every file is mono PCM WAV
Every file starts at silence (first sample under 1% of peak) and ends in silence (last 5 ms under 1% of peak) and does not clip
Running the generator script a second time produces byte-identical files
Peaks are consistent across the set: the loudest and quietest of the six non-blip effects are within 6 dB of each other, and the talk blip is quieter than the win/lose jingles
The win and lose effects are short jingles with pitched notes (several distinct pitches), the lose one descending or in a minor/dark character
The sounds are synthesised in Python (numpy or similar), not downloaded or sampled from existing audio
The script has one function or entry per effect with a short description of the sound, and its randomness is seeded deterministically (one seed, or one constant per effect)
